steps.title: Electrolysis
steps.body: The process of using electricity to break down an ionic compound into its elements. The compound must be molten or dissolved in water (aqueous) so that ions can move.

steps.title: Electrolyte
steps.body: The ionic compound that is broken down by electrolysis. It must be molten or in solution so the ions are free to move.

steps.title: Anode
steps.body: The positive electrode. Negative ions (anions) are attracted here and lose electrons (oxidation).

steps.title: Cathode
steps.body: The negative electrode. Positive ions (cations) are attracted here and gain electrons (reduction).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: In aqueous solutions, water is also present. The ions from water (H⁺ and OH⁻) compete with the ions from the dissolved compound. This means different products can form depending on which ions are discharged. Rules for aqueous solutions: At the cathode: If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen gas (H₂) is produced instead. If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen, the metal is produced. At the anode: If halide ions (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) are present, the halogen is produced. If no halide ions are present, oxygen (O₂) is produced from hydroxide ions. steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Foundation Define electrolysis. What type of current is used? | Foundation Predict the products at each electrode when molten potassium iodide is electrolysed. | Higher Predict the products at each electrode when copper(II) chloride solution is electrolysed. Write the half-equations.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Electrolysis is the process of using electricity to break down an ionic compound into its elements. A direct current (DC) is used. | Cathode: potassium (K). Anode: iodine (I₂). The K⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode and gain electrons. The I⁻ ions are attracted to the anode and lose electrons. | Cathode: copper — Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (Cu is less reactive than H). Anode: chlorine — 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (Cl⁻ is a halide ion).

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Remember: cathode is negative (attracts cations), anode is positive (attracts anions) For aqueous electrolysis, always check if the metal is above or below hydrogen in the reactivity series Learn the rule: reactive metals → hydrogen at cathode; unreactive metals → metal at cathode For the anode: halides come first. If no halide is present, oxygen is produced Half-equations must balance — make sure the number of electrons lost at the anode equals the number gained at the cathode In aluminium extraction, remember the anodes burn away (C + O₂ → CO₂) and need replacing In electroplating questions, the object being plated is always the cathode
